answer.evidence: The silhouette is a full 96-wide opaque rectangle on every row (0-95), so this is a seamless tile and not a standing object. Rows repeat a brick pattern: dark mortar lines at rows 3, 11, 19, 27, 35 and so on, a lighter bevel line just below each mortar row, and a darker row beneath. Every brick looks the same and is a flat texture. No brick course ends in an eave or front-edge line, there is no receding side face, and there is no separate south face. The medallion at rows 33-62 is a flat circle seen straight on, with no depth. The tile is a flat floor surface with no front face, so the structural rule decides the result, not me.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a grey brick floor with a rune medallion. Its measured facts match the paving reference: 7 visible tones per tile against 7, and 0% near-flat coverage against 0%. Each brick has a light top edge, a mid face, a darker lower edge and dark mortar, plus a few speckle dots, so it reads as about 5 steps against the paving's 6. The dark edge pixels are 100% neutral against 80% for the paving. Here that comes from the grey stone ramp itself, because the mortar is the dark tone of the adjacent grey brick rather than a black sticker outline. The medallion has a tinted gold and blue rim. The brick rhythm is more regular and mechanical than the hand-shaded stones in the paving reference, so I rate density slightly lower, but it is not shallow and a careful artist could place it next to the reference.

surfaces.part: circular rune medallion with gold rim, inlaid in the floor

answer.evidence: The whole 96x96 tile is a flat, running-bond pattern of stone slabs with dark mortar lines. Every row is the same full width of 96 pixels. There is no front-edge line, no eave shadow and no vertical south face. The gold medallion spans about 29 columns by 30 rows (rows 33-62), so it is a circle seen straight down, not a foreshortened ellipse. It is an inlaid ornament, not a standing part. The tile reads as a plain top-down floor surface with no front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The measured facts put the candidate level with the paving reference at 7 visible tones per tile, with 0% near-flat coverage, so it is not a flat fill. By eye, though, the floor is a regular grid of grey bricks. Each brick has about 4 steps: a light top edge, a mid face, a darker lower edge and a mortar line, with only sparse speckle. The reference paving shades its cobbles one by one, with bright chiselled edges, dark gaps and a grainy surface, which gives about 6 steps. The candidate's dark pixels are 100% neutral grey with no tint, and the mortar lines run as an even uniform grid. That reads as a sticker-like outline rather than the material-tinted, selective edging Beodeul uses. The brick pattern repeats with little variation between bricks. The central medallion is a clean, well-made focal element, but it does not add richness to the floor surface. Next to the reference the floor looks thinner and more mechanical.
